items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the retirement and social security law, the administrative code of the city of New York, and the general municipal law, in relation to the disability benefits of members of the New York city police and fire pension funds
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5596

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the retirement and social security law, the administra-
tive code of the city of New York, and the general municipal law, in
relation to the disability benefits of members of the New York city
police and fire pension funds

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section one of this bill amends section 1205 of the Retirement and
Social Security Law to reopen the election for those members who joined
the New York State and Local Police and Fire Retirement System pursuant
to the provisions of Article 14 of the Retirement and Social Security
Law so that those members who did not previously elect to have their
benefits calculated pursuant to Article 22 to make such an election.

Section two of this bill amends sections 13-357(a) and 13-357(b) of the
Administrative Code of New York City, subdivision (a) as amended by the
Laws of 1986, to include disability pensioners who have retired pursuant
to Section 506 and Section 507 of the Retirement and Social Security
Law.

Section three of this bill adds subdivisions (e) and (f) to Section 506
of the Retirement and Social Security Law. Subdivisions (e) and (f)
respectively allow New York City fire and police pension fund members to
be eligible for ordinary disability retirement benefits pursuant to
sections 13-216, 13-251, 13-252, 13-254, 13-316 or 13-357 of the New
York City Administrative Code, as applicable to the retiring member. A
member who retires under any of these Administrative Code provisions
shall receive an annuity equal to his or her accumulated contributions,
a pension equal to the reserve-for-increased-take-home-pay for him or
her, and a pension equal to one-fortieth of his or her final average
salary multiplied by the number of years of city-service credited to him
or her but not less than half of his or her Final Average Salary ("FAS")
if his or her credited years are ten or more, or one-third of his or her
FAS if his or her credited years are less than ten.

Section four of this bill adds subdivisions (j) and (k) to Section 507
of the Retirement and Social Security Law. Subdivisions (j) and (k)
respectively allow New York City fire and police pension fund members to
be eligible for accidental disability retirement pursuant to sections
13-215, 13-252, 13-254, 13-316, 13-353- 13-354, or 13-357 of the New
York City Administrative Code. These new subdivisions provide that a
retiree shall receive an annuity equal to his or her accumulated
contributions, a pension equal to the reserve-for-increased-take-home-
pay for him or her, and a pension equal to 75 percent of his or her FAS.

Section five of this bill adds subdivision (i) to Section 510 of the
Retirement and Social Security Law. Subdivision (i) provides that annual
escalation shall not apply to the ordinary or accidental disability

retirement benefits for those who retire pursuant to Sections 506 and
507 of the Retirement and Social Security Law.  Instead, their benefits
shall be adjusted for cost-of-living pursuant to Section 13-696 of the
New York City Administrative Code.

Section six of this bill amends Section 511(f) of the Retirement and
Social Security Law to provide that this section shall not apply to New
York City police and fire pension members who are subject to Article 14
of the Retirement and Social Security Law.

Section seven of this bill adds subdivisions (e) and (f) to Section 512
of the Retirement and Social Security Law. Subdivisions (e) and (f)
respectively provide that New York City fire and police pension members
FAS shall mean the salary earned the year prior to retirement, unless
that salary is 20 percent more than the year prior to that, in which
case that excess 20 percent is excluded from the FAS computation.
Authorized leaves of absence shall be excluded from the FAS computation
as well.

Section eight of this bill reletters paragraph (b) of Section
13-353.1(1) of the New York City Administrative Code to (c) and adds a
new paragraph (b). New paragraph (b) states that in order to be eligible
for the World Trade Center presumption provided by paragraph (a) of this
subdivision, a member must have passed a physical exam for entry into
public service that failed to disclose evidence of the qualifying condi-
tion that is the basis for the disability, or have authorized for the
release of medical records if he or she did not have a physical exam for
entry into public service and there is no evidence in those records that
the qualifying condition that serves as the basis for the disability
existed before September 11, 2001.

Section nine of this bill amends section 207-k of the General Municipal
Law to extend the current presumption for diseases of the heart and
strokes to medical officers employed by the New York City fire depart-
ment.

Section ten of this bill amends section 207-kk of the General Municipal
Law to extend the current presumption for certain cancers to medical
officers employed by the New York City fire department.

Section eleven of this bill amends section 207-p of the General Munici-
pal Law to extend the current presumption for HIV to medical officers
employed by the New York City fire department.

Section twelve of this bill amends section 207-q of the General Munici-
pal Law to extend the current presumption for lung diseases to medical
officers employed by the New York City fire department.

Section thirteen of this bill provides that this act shall take effect
on the sixtieth day after it shall become a law; provided, however, that
amendments to sections 207-k, 207-kk and 207-q of the general municipal
law made by sections nine, ten and twelve of this act shall not affect

the expiration of such sections, as provided in section 480 of the
retirement and social security law.

JUSTIFICATION:

In 2009, Governor Paterson vetoed a Tier 2 extension bill for all New
York State Police and Fire pension members. In Veto Memorandum 5, Gover-
nor Paterson stated that due to the "recession and fiscal crisis," as
well as the Comptroller's announcement that the "New York State Pension
Fund lost 26% of its value in the most recent fiscal year," led to his
decision not to "ignore the present reality, and simply re-enact the
same provisions that have contributed to New York's financial straits,
without accompanying reform." This reform, which was Tier V, was
approved on December 10, 2009 as Chapter 504 of the Laws of 2009.

Shortly after Governor Paterson issued Veto Memorandum 5, most of the
State Police and Fire unions negotiated with management and agreed to a
Tier V benefit plan. Members of these unions that were hired on or after
July 1, 2009 were provided with the option to change the calculation of
their retirement benefits from Article 14 of the Retirement and Social
Security Law to Article 22. For those members continue to have their
retirement benefits computed pursuant to Article 14 of the Retirement
and Social Security Law, this bill would reopen the option that was
available when Tier V was enacted. Tier V was not welcomed warmly. There
were mixed reports regarding whether Tier V was beneficial to the
members. Reopening this option is important because as the years have
gone by, members who failed opt into Article 22 for whatever reason,
whether it be confusion regarding what the election meant or the differ-
ences between Articles 14 and 22, may wish to make such an election.

The Mayor of New York City would not agree to the same Tier V benefits,
resulting in no new pension plan agreement covering New York City Police
and Fire members. With no new pension plan, New York City Police and
Fire members defaulted into the original Article 14 Tier III pension
plan. Tier III provides very limited disability benefits, which are only
50% of the member's final average salary, which is reduced by 50% of the
primary social security benefit received. Tier II members receive an
accidental disability benefit equaling 75% of the member's final average
salary with no reduction for primary social security benefits received
by the member.

An example in the difference in these benefits is illustrated by the
potential accidental disability benefits that would be provided to
Police Officer Kenneth Healey. On October 23, 2014, by a man wielding an
18 inch hatchet struck Officer Healey in the head while he was standing
on a sidewalk with three other police officers in Jamaica, Queens. As a
result of the attack Officer Healy was hospitalized for five days and
has underwent two surgeries on his skull. If Officer Healy received an
accidental disability pension due to his injuries, the amount of the
pension would be approximately $21,000 per year, with a reduction in an
amount equaling 50% of any primary social security benefits that he may
receive. If Officer Healy was eligible to receive Tier II accidental

disability benefits, he would receive approximately $31,500 per year
without any reduction for social security benefits.

Another example of this inequity is illustrated by the potential acci-
dental disability benefits that would be paid to Police Officer Rosa
Rodriguez. Officer Rodriguez was injured when she and her partner
responded to an apartment fire in Coney Island that was set by a teenag-
er. She and her partner, Police Officer Dennis Guerra, were overcome by
smoke in the burning building. They were both rushed to the hospital in
critical condition Officer Guerra died four days later as a result of
his injuries. Officer Rodriguez was in a coma for six days and has been
released from the hospital with an uncertain future because the doctors
have said that she may never fully recover from her injuries. Officer
Rodriguez would be entitled to an accidental disability pension of
$22,000 per year, with a reduction in an amount equaling 50% of any
primary social security benefits that she may receive. If Officer Rodri-
guez was eligible to receive Tier II accidental disability benefits, she
would receive approximately $31,500 per year without any reduction for
social security benefits.

This bill would reverse the inequities inherent in Tier III illustrated
by Officer Healy and Officer Rodriguez

This bill would further recognize that the medical officers employed by
the New York City Fire Department frequently respond to fires, and thus,
should be afforded the same presumptions for medical impairments that
can lead to disability or death as firefighters. Dr.  Kerry Kelly and
Dr. David Prezant were medical officers with the New York City Fire
Department on September 11, 2001 when they responded to the need for
medical assistance at the World trade Center. This bill would afford
them World Trade Center presumption for qualifying conditions should
they become disabled or die from a qualifying condition. These medical
officers respond to help those who are injured when a fire breaks out
They are right there on the front lines, and thus, should be afforded
the same presumptions for medical impairments that are currently granted
to firefighters.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

This is a new bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

See the bill.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

This act shall take effect on the sixtieth day after it shall become a
law; provided, however, that amendments to sections 207-k, 207-kk and
207-q of the general municipal law made by sections nine, ten and twelve
of this act shall not affect the expiration of such sections, as
provided in section 480 of the retirement and social security law.
